beats.script_body: The New Museum's building is the brainchild of Japanese firm SANAA — a partnership between Kazuyo Sejima and Ryue Nishizawa. In 2010, SANAA won the coveted Pritzker Prize (think the Oscars of architecture) for its contributions to the world of design. Their trademark vanishing facades are known worldwide for abiding by a strict adherence to a form-follows-function design aesthetic, sometimes taking the land plot's footprint into the overall shape of the structure. The box-atop-box scheme provides a striking counterpoint to the clusters of crimson brick and iron fire escapes outside, while alluding to the geometric exhibition chasms within.

beats.script_body: The 'Hard Times' tour, one of the most popular, visits apartments from two periods — the 1870s and the 1930s. There you'll see the squalid conditions tenants faced: in the early days there was a wretched communal outhouse and no electricity or running water. beats.script_body: The 10.5-acre Tompkins Square Park honors Daniel Tompkins, who served as governor of New York from 1807 to 1817, and as the nation's vice president after that, under James Monroe. Dating from 1879, the park is like a friendly town square for locals, who gather for chess at concrete tables, picnics on the lawn, and spontaneous guitar or drum jams on various grassy knolls. It also has basketball courts, a fun-to-watch dog run, a mini public swimming pool for kids, and frequent summer concerts.

beats.script_body: In the 1980s the park was a dirty, needle-strewn homeless encampment, unusable for folks wanting a place to stroll or picnic. A contentious turning point came when police razed the band shell and evicted more than 100 squatters living in a tent city in 1988 — and again in 1991. That first eviction turned violent: the Tompkins Square Riot ushered in the first wave of yuppies in the dog run, fashionistas lolling on the grass, and undercover narcotics agents trying to pass as druggie punk kids.

beats.source_passage: In the 1980s it was a dirty, needle-strewn, homeless encampment, unusable for folks wanting a place to stroll or picnic. A contentious turning point came when police razed the band shell and evicted more than 100 squatters living in a tent city in the park in 1988 (and again in 1991). That first eviction turned violent; the Tompkins Square Riot, as it came to be known, ushered in the first wave of yuppies in the dog run, fashionistas lolling on the grass and undercover narcotics agents trying to pass as druggie punk kids.

beats.script_body: These days there's not much drama in Tompkins Square Park, outside of the occasional music and arts festival that attempts to briefly reclaim the park's bohemian glory days — such as the Charlie Parker Jazz Festival held here every August.
